prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We analyze 27 house price indexes of Las Vegas from Jun. 1983 to Mar. 2005, corresponding to 27 different zip codes. These analyses confirm the existence of a real-estate bubble, defined as a price acceleration faster than exponential, which is found however to be confined to a rather limited time interval in the recent past from approximately 2003 to mid-2004 and has progressively transformed into a more normal growth rate comparable to pre-bubble levels in 2005. There has been no bubble till 2002 except for a medium-sized surge in 1990. In addition, we have identified a strong yearly periodicity which provides a good potential for fine-tuned prediction from month to month. A monthly monitoring using a model that we have developed could confirm, by testing the intra-year structure, if indeed the market has returned to ``normal'' or if more turbulence is expected ahead. We predict the evolution of the indexes one year ahead, which is validated with new data up to Sep. 2006. The present analysis demonstrates the existence of very significant variations at the local scale, in the sense that the bubble in Las Vegas seems to have preceded the more global USA bubble and has ended approximately two years earlier (mid 2004 for Las Vegas compared with mid-2006 for the whole of the USA).

outputs.L1:
We analyze 27 Las Vegas house price indexes from June 1983 to March 2005, each corresponding to a different ZIP code. Our analyses confirm the existence of a real-estate bubble, defined as price acceleration at a faster-than-exponential rate. However, the bubble appears to have been confined to a relatively brief period, from approximately 2003 to mid-2004, after which price appreciation progressively returned to a more normal rate, comparable to pre-bubble levels, in 2005. We find no evidence of a bubble before 2002, apart from a moderate surge in 1990.

In addition, we identify a strong annual periodicity that offers considerable potential for fine-tuned month-to-month forecasting. Monthly monitoring using a model we have developed could determine, by testing the intra-year structure, whether the market has indeed returned to “normal” or whether further turbulence lies ahead. We forecast the evolution of the indexes one year ahead and validate these predictions using new data through September 2006.

The present analysis reveals highly significant variations at the local scale: the Las Vegas bubble appears to have preceded the broader U.S. real-estate bubble and to have ended approximately two years earlier—mid-2004 in Las Vegas, compared with mid-2006 for the United States as a whole.

We examine 27 Las Vegas housing-price indexes, each representing a different ZIP code, over the period from June 1983 through March 2005. The results support the presence of a real-estate bubble—understood as price growth accelerating beyond an exponential rate. However, this bubble appears to have been restricted to a relatively short recent period, roughly from 2003 to mid-2004. By 2005, price increases had gradually slowed to a more typical pace similar to that observed before the bubble. No bubble is evident before 2002, aside from a moderate price surge in 1990.

We also detect a pronounced annual cycle that could enable precise month-to-month forecasting. Monthly tracking with our model could use this within-year pattern to determine whether the market has truly returned to “normal” conditions or whether further instability lies ahead. We forecast the indexes one year into the future and validate those projections using additional observations extending through September 2006.

Overall, the study reveals substantial variation at the local level. In particular, the Las Vegas bubble appears to have begun before the broader U.S. housing bubble and to have ended about two years sooner—around mid-2004 in Las Vegas, versus mid-2006 nationwide.

The study examines 27 house price indexes for Las Vegas ZIP codes, covering the period from June 1983 to March 2005. Its findings indicate that the city experienced a real-estate bubble—defined by house prices rising at a faster-than-exponential rate—primarily between 2003 and mid-2004. After this peak period, price growth began moving back toward its pre-bubble trajectory in 2005.

The analysis found no clear evidence of a bubble before 2002, although a moderate price surge occurred around 1990. It also identified a strong annual periodic pattern in housing prices. This seasonality could support month-to-month forecasting and provide a useful tool for continuously monitoring changes in local real-estate markets.

Importantly, the bubble did not affect all parts of Las Vegas uniformly. The timing and intensity of price increases varied substantially across ZIP codes, highlighting the importance of neighborhood-level analysis. Overall, the Las Vegas housing bubble appeared before the broader U.S. housing bubble and ended approximately two years earlier. Forecasts based on the study’s models were subsequently evaluated against additional housing data through September 2006, providing an out-of-sample test of their accuracy.

The study examines monthly house-price indexes for 27 ZIP codes in the Las Vegas metropolitan area from June 1983 through March 2005. Its objective is to determine whether the city’s rapid housing appreciation represented a speculative bubble, to establish when that bubble began and ended, and to assess whether a nonlinear model could produce reliable out-of-sample price forecasts. The model allows prices to rise faster than exponentially—a key indicator of unsustainable growth—while also accounting for recurring annual seasonality in the housing market.

The results show that the bubble was both geographically and temporally concentrated. Most of the abnormal acceleration occurred between 2003 and the middle of 2004, and it was especially pronounced in a limited number of ZIP codes rather than appearing uniformly across the entire metropolitan area. By early 2005, estimated growth rates had largely returned to more typical levels, indicating that the explosive phase had already ended even though prices could remain elevated or continue moving for some time afterward.

Forecasts based on data available through March 2005 were subsequently compared with observed prices through September 2006. Their performance supports the model’s ability to distinguish temporary faster-than-exponential appreciation from ordinary market growth and seasonal variation. Taken together, the evidence suggests that Las Vegas experienced a distinct local housing bubble whose principal expansion and normalization occurred roughly two years before the peak and reversal of the broader U.S. housing bubble.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the key findings of a study analyzing house price indexes across 27 Las Vegas zip codes from 1983 to 2006.
counterfactuals.output:
The study found that Las Vegas did not operate as a single, fully integrated housing market during 1983–2006:

- House-price indexes for the 27 ZIP codes generally moved together over the long run, reflecting common metropolitan-wide forces such as population growth, employment, interest rates, and credit conditions.
- Price changes were spatially uneven. Some ZIP codes—typically established, higher-priced areas—tended to lead, with appreciation subsequently spreading to nearby or less-expensive neighborhoods, consistent with a “ripple effect.”
- The ZIP-code indexes showed strong persistence, and relative price gaps could remain for long periods. Evidence of convergence was therefore limited or occurred in subgroups rather than uniformly across all 27 areas.
- Geographic proximity alone did not fully explain the relationships; neighborhood characteristics and market segmentation also mattered.
- The rapid boom in the early 2000s intensified co-movement but also produced unusually large departures from historical relationships, indicating that short-run speculative or demand shocks could overwhelm normal adjustment patterns.

Overall, the analysis highlights the importance of using neighborhood-level data: a metropolitan average conceals substantial differences in the timing, magnitude, and transmission of house-price changes across Las Vegas.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an academic abstract about detecting a faster-than-exponential real-estate bubble in Las Vegas using monthly housing price data, including seasonality, forecasts, and comparison with the broader U.S. housing bubble.
counterfactuals.output: This study examines whether the rapid appreciation of Las Vegas residential property prices constitutes a faster-than-exponential speculative bubble. Using monthly housing price data, we first decompose the series to account for recurring seasonal variation and then evaluate its long-run growth dynamics. Bubble detection is conducted with a log-periodic power-law singularity framework, which distinguishes super-exponential price acceleration from conventional exponential growth and estimates a probabilistic window for the regime’s termination. Out-of-sample forecasts from seasonal time-series benchmarks are compared with bubble-model projections to assess whether recent price movements exceed levels justified by historical trends and seasonal patterns. The Las Vegas results are then contrasted with those for the broader U.S. housing market, enabling an assessment of whether local dynamics represent an amplified manifestation of the national cycle or a distinct metropolitan bubble. The analysis finds stronger evidence of faster-than-exponential growth and greater forecast divergence in Las Vegas than at the national level, consistent with the city’s comparatively high sensitivity to speculative demand, migration, and credit conditions. The findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating seasonality and model uncertainty when identifying real-estate bubbles and provide an empirical framework for monitoring local housing-market instability relative to aggregate U.S. conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What did researchers conclude about the timing, duration, and geographic variation of the Las Vegas housing bubble, and how did it compare with the nationwide U.S. bubble?
counterfactuals.output:
Researchers found that Las Vegas’s housing bubble was unusually **late, short, and intense**. It generally emerged around **2003**, after the broader U.S. boom was already underway, and ended around **2006**, giving it a duration of roughly three years.

The timing was not uniform within the metropolitan area: different ZIP codes or neighborhoods entered and exited the bubble at different times, with substantial variation in duration and intensity as speculative price growth spread across the valley.

By comparison, the **nationwide U.S. housing bubble began in the late 1990s and lasted until about 2006–07**. Thus, Las Vegas largely shared the national turning point, but its run-up started later, was more compressed, and was considerably more dramatic.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Using data from June 1983 through March 2005 for 27 Las Vegas ZIP-code house price indexes, describe whether a housing bubble existed, identify any yearly periodicity, and explain how one-year-ahead predictions were validated through September 2006.
counterfactuals.output:
- **Bubble evidence.** The 27 monthly Case–Shiller–Weiss ZIP-code indexes moved together and showed a marked, faster-than-exponential acceleration beginning around 2003, with extraordinary appreciation in 2004. This broad synchronization and unsustainable acceleration were interpreted as a speculative Las Vegas housing bubble. By early 2005, however, appreciation rates had already turned down sharply, indicating a transition from the bubble regime to a slower-growth or flattening regime—not necessarily an immediate price crash.

- **Annual periodicity.** Analysis of monthly changes after removing the long-run trend revealed a statistically clear **12-month seasonal cycle**, along with weaker harmonics. Appreciation was generally stronger during the spring and summer selling season and weaker around late fall and winter. The seasonality was common across most ZIP codes and was incorporated into forecasting rather than mistaken for renewed bubble growth.

- **One-year-ahead forecasts and validation.** Using only observations available through **March 2005**, the authors fitted the post-bubble trend together with the recurring seasonal component and issued ZIP-level forecasts for **April 2005–March 2006**. These were genuine out-of-sample predictions: parameters were not re-estimated with the later observations. When subsequently released index data became available, the forecasts were compared with realized values, while data through **September 2006** supplied an additional six-month check on the predicted regime. The later data broadly confirmed the forecast of pronounced deceleration/near-plateauing and retained seasonality, although accuracy varied among ZIP codes and the indexes themselves were subject to later revision.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper abstract reporting an analysis of Las Vegas home prices that defines a bubble as faster-than-exponential price acceleration, dates the local bubble to roughly 2003–mid-2004, notes the 1990 surge and annual seasonality, and discusses monthly monitoring and forecasting.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—**This study analyzes the dynamics of Las Vegas residential real-estate prices, defining a speculative bubble as a period of faster-than-exponential price acceleration rather than merely rapid appreciation. Using monthly home-price data, we identify a local bubble that emerged around 2003 and persisted until approximately mid-2004, after which price growth slowed from its unsustainable trajectory. The historical series also reveals a pronounced price surge around 1990 and a recurring annual seasonal pattern, underscoring the need to distinguish short-lived shocks and calendar effects from genuine bubble dynamics. The results demonstrate how monthly estimation can support near-real-time monitoring of market conditions, facilitate early detection of super-exponential growth, and improve short-horizon forecasting. More broadly, the analysis suggests that combining bubble diagnostics with explicit treatment of seasonality and earlier price episodes provides a practical framework for tracking rapidly changing metropolitan housing markets.
